title: Electronics and control: three responsibilities, one board.
summary: Engine management, vehicle control and shared electrical integration form the proposed electronics architecture. Define their boundaries before selecting the hardware.
heroAlt: Electronics and control: three responsibilities, one board. — conceptual functional diagram
heroCaption: R01 proposed architecture. Not a wiring, manufacturing or validated control specification. Open the diagram for full-size inspection.

sections.title: Research stage, not a finished control system
sections.text: Electronic fuel injection is a Wahoo requirement. The proposed 125 cc single-cylinder two-stroke engine and approximately 12,000 rpm research target guide this investigation; the final operating envelope remains open. R01 records no integrated controller, completed calibration, marine qualification or adaptive riding test.

sections.title: Engine management and vehicle control are siblings
sections.text: Engine management (EMS) brings the ECU, fuel injection, ignition and engine instrumentation together. Vehicle control (VCS) interprets board motion and records riding conditions. Shared electrical integration supplies protected power, communications, connectors and the harness. The ECU is a component of EMS; the VCS is a separate development package.

sections.title: The working shortlist
sections.text: R01 identifies MaxxECU SPORT plus a Teensy 4.1 VCS prototype as the provisional development combination, with intake EFI as the working injection arrangement. This is a shortlist for investigation, not a production selection or a claim of demonstrated compatibility. MaxxECU documents two-stroke support, electronic throttle capability and CAN; those features still require application-specific confirmation. S01 · Manufacturer specifications.

sections.title: What could change the choice
sections.text: Retaining mechanical throttle may reduce the first prototype’s ECU requirements. Selecting chamber direct injection reopens the injector driver, pressure, timing and lubrication decisions. Packaging, power consumption, available external commands and written high-speed trigger support can also change the shortlist.

table.caption: R01 candidate roles — application approval remains open
rows: Exact trigger, injector, ignition, external requests and marine installation.
Alternatives for a simpler first engine milestone

Development, calibration, support and qualification effort; no reliability ranking.

sections.title: Decisions remain connected to the physical board
sections.text: Engine geometry sets trigger and sensor interfaces. Fuel tank pickup and return routing affect pressure stability. Exhaust layout affects temperature and mixture instrumentation. Pump behaviour shapes any future unloading detection. Moving-nozzle coordination remains a future interface: actuator, position feedback, loads and control law are unselected.

sections.title: Separate development cost from production cost
sections.text: A processor board price is not the cost of a working VCS. The scope includes a transceiver, protected supply, sensors, wiring, connectors, enclosure, firmware, calibration and testing. R01 contains dated retail observations, but no complete installed electronics cost or achieved production bill of materials. Procurement needs written, like-for-like quotations.

sections.title: Read the packages in order
sections.text: Start with engine management, then vehicle control, electrical integration and the validation plan. These records explain requirements and proposed work; none reports a completed electronics test.

title: Engine management: fuel, spark and five milliseconds.
summary: Investigate EFI, ignition, event timing and sensor dependencies together. At the proposed 12,000 rpm reference speed, a two-stroke cycle lasts just 5 milliseconds.
heroAlt: Engine management: fuel, spark and five milliseconds. — conceptual functional diagram
heroCaption: R01 proposed architecture. Not a wiring, manufacturing or validated control specification. Open the diagram for full-size inspection.

sections.title: The ECU works inside a larger system
sections.text: Crank position provides the timing reference. Rider demand and engine measurements inform a calibrated injection and ignition strategy. Output drivers must match the injector and ignition hardware; a logic-level output is not necessarily a power stage for a bare coil. Fuel pickup, pump, filter and regulator must maintain the required delivery independently of the software.

sections.title: EFI does not automatically mean direct injection
sections.text: Intake EFI is the provisional baseline. Transfer-port injection and chamber direct injection remain alternatives. Only an injector spraying directly into the combustion chamber establishes chamber DI. Each route changes packaging, fuel preparation, injection timing and lubrication; a conventional intake injector driver is not approval for a high-pressure DI injector.

sections.title: The timing budget at high speed
sections.text: At 12,000 rpm, the crankshaft makes 200 revolutions per second. A two-stroke cycle therefore lasts 60,000 / 12,000 = 5.00 ms; each crank degree takes approximately 13.9 microseconds. These are calculated references, not a selected calibration.

table.caption: Calculated timing examples — no injection schedule selected
rows: One spark per cycle at 12,000 rpm

sections.title: Select the injector and driver as a pair
sections.text: Required inputs include the fuel-demand envelope, pressure, permitted duty or angular window, opening behaviour versus voltage, short-pulse response and spray geometry. Displacement alone does not establish injector flow. Bosch EV14 is a family for investigation, not an approved part number. The injector, throttle body, coil and regulator remain unselected.

sections.title: Lubrication follows the injection decision
sections.text: Changing where fuel enters can change whether oil carried with it reaches the crankshaft and bearings. Premix compatibility, separate metering and the implications of fuel-cut strategies require explicit review. Electronic injection does not provide lubrication by itself. Generic automotive tuning features are not automatically suitable for this engine.

sections.title: Keep critical measurements at the ECU
sections.text: Crank timing, rider/throttle demand, intake conditions, engine temperature, fuel pressure and supply voltage form the proposed engine measurement set. EGT requires a matching thermocouple interface; SPORT does not include an EGT input. Lambda measurement needs compatible electronics and a valid installation. Two-stroke scavenging and wet exhaust conditions complicate interpretation.

table.caption: Proposed engine instrumentation — exact sensors and limits open
rows: Demand measurement and plausibility where electronic throttle is used.
Air temperature / ambient pressure / intake pressure
Compensation and investigation of intake pulsation.
Separate fuel-supply and electrical faults from calibration issues.
Mixture investigation only under a valid installation and operating method.

sections.title: The first milestone is repeatability
sections.text: Starting, stable synchronisation, predictable injection, controlled ignition and a functioning stop path take priority over riding intelligence. No power gain, fuel-consumption reduction, temperature limit or injector sizing result is established in this research record.

title: Vehicle control: observe first, request later.
summary: A separate VCS would record motion and engine behaviour before any bounded riding intervention is evaluated. Engine protection remains with the ECU.
heroAlt: Vehicle control: observe first, request later. — conceptual functional diagram
heroCaption: R01 proposed architecture. Not a wiring, manufacturing or validated control specification. Open the diagram for full-size inspection.

sections.title: A logger before a riding controller
sections.text: The proposed VCS combines engine data with board motion and navigation measurements. Teensy 4.1 is the provisional logging prototype platform; it still needs protected power, signal interfaces and a CAN transceiver. ESP32 or STM32 development platforms remain alternatives. None of these development boards is a qualified marine controller.

sections.title: Requests are not engine authority
sections.text: The VCS may eventually request a permitted mode or bounded limit. The ECU must retain the defined engine-protection functions and critical inputs. Loss of the VCS must not produce an uncontrolled demand increase. A sudden reduction also has handling consequences, so the fallback must be specified and tested for the operating state.

sections.title: CAN is a transport, not a shared language
sections.text: Both ends need matching message definitions. The proposed contract includes identifiers, units, scaling, byte order, ranges, update periods, timeouts and receiver actions. ECU-to-VCS measurements and VCS-to-ECU requests need separate definitions. A transceiver does not translate incompatible application protocols.

sections.title: A zero value is not automatically a safe fallback
sections.text: MaxxECU documents timeout zeroing for a CAN input. What zero means depends on the receiving strategy. Missing, stale, corrupt, out-of-range and rapidly changing messages therefore need explicit tests. Request freshness and validity must be evaluated separately from the request value. S07 · CAN input documentation.

sections.title: Measure before interpreting
sections.text: An IMU measures acceleration and angular rate; it does not directly identify a corner, jump or cavitation event. GNSS adds speed and route context, while optional cooling, ingress, fuel-level and future nozzle-position measurements answer different questions. Candidate sensors and their locations need vibration, interference and calibration checks.

table.caption: Proposed vehicle measurements
rows: Can repeatable ride events be identified despite vibration and mounting effects?
How do speed and route align with rider demand and engine events?
Cooling flow or pressure / water temperature
Can useful cooling conditions and loss of cooling be distinguished?
Can leakage or low fuel be detected without misleading motion-induced readings?
If an actuator proceeds, does its measured position match the request?

sections.title: Riding strategies remain experiments
sections.text: Launch response, cornering, rough-water demand progression and pump-unloading limits are research topics. An RPM flare alone does not prove cavitation: ventilation, loss of immersion and airborne operation can also unload the pump. Any intervention needs labelled test data, confidence checks, bounded response and controlled recovery. Beginner, Sport and Race are possible names, not specifications.

sections.title: Keep wireless outside essential control
sections.text: A phone interface or log-transfer module may support service, but engine operation and stopping must not depend on wireless connectivity. Autonomous navigation, computer vision and unrestricted automatic generation of fuel or ignition maps are outside R01’s established requirements.

title: Electrical integration: power, harness and marine exposure.
summary: The controller is only one part of the installation. Starting transients, sensor returns, connectors, sealing and service access must be designed and tested together.
heroAlt: Electrical integration: power, harness and marine exposure. — conceptual functional diagram
heroCaption: R01 proposed architecture. Not a wiring, manufacturing or validated control specification. Open the diagram for full-size inspection.

sections.title: Define the electrical operating envelope
sections.text: The proposed distribution separates starter, engine-control and protected low-voltage electronics branches. The battery’s cranking minimum, charging maximum and transient behaviour matter alongside nominal voltage. R01 deliberately selects no fuse ratings, wire sizes or battery capacity.

sections.title: Protect measurement integrity
sections.text: Branch protection must be matched to wiring and loads. Sensitive sensor returns, starter currents and ignition paths need a documented grounding and routing strategy. The crank signal and measurement wiring must be assessed for interference. The harness drawing must define shielding and termination rather than leaving them to installation improvisation.

sections.title: A development board is not a battery interface
sections.text: The VCS needs a suitable regulator and input protection. Automotive sensors may also require level conversion or protected interfaces: Teensy’s 3.3 V input limits cannot be treated as permission to connect an arbitrary 5 V signal. Power disturbance and reset behaviour belong in the bench test plan.

sections.title: Stop and restart are system functions
sections.text: The lanyard/stop path must not depend on a phone, GNSS or the high-level VCS application. The exact stop chain depends on the chosen ECU and ignition arrangement. Starter permission, running lockout, pump shutdown and unintended-restart inhibition must be demonstrated; branch separation alone does not establish independence.

sections.title: Qualify the assembled installation
sections.text: Water, salt, vibration, shock and heat act on the complete enclosure, connectors, harness, mounting and electronics. A connector-family rating or processor specification is not evidence that the assembled board is marine-qualified.

table.caption: Proposed environmental review — acceptance conditions still to be defined
rows: Exact parts, mating state, unused-cavity sealing and assembled exposure tests.
Material compatibility, sealing-surface inspection and service procedure.
Representative mounting loads, strain relief and measured test profiles.
Controller and driver temperatures in the actual sealed enclosure.
No timing corruption or unintended reset during starter and switched-load tests.
Repeatable diagnosis without damaging seals or changing calibration.

sections.title: Make serviceability a design decision
sections.text: Coating, selective encapsulation and full potting have different repair and heat-transfer consequences. A vent needs its own exposure assessment. Exposed USB or magnetic connectors are not automatically suitable for wet mating or saltwater; a protected internal service connection may be simpler for the prototype.

sections.title: Cost the complete package
sections.text: Include protection electronics, interfaces, cable and connector assemblies, housings, diagnostic access, firmware, calibration and environmental tests. Retail controller and processor-board prices do not establish the installed system cost. No production cost saving has been demonstrated in R01.

title: Electronics validation: from bench signals to bounded water tests.
summary: Five proposed validation gates separate component research, bench checks, engine calibration, logging-only water trials and later control interventions.
heroAlt: Electronics validation: from bench signals to bounded water tests. — conceptual functional diagram
heroCaption: R01 proposed architecture. Not a wiring, manufacturing or validated control specification. Open the diagram for full-size inspection.

sections.title: A plan, not a test-results dashboard
sections.text: This R01 record describes proposed gates and evidence requirements. No gate is presented as passed. Firmware, wiring, calibration and sensor-location changes require a review of which earlier results remain applicable.

sections.title: Five gates before adaptive control
sections.text: First confirm the exact engine, trigger, injector, ignition, sensor and supply requirements with suppliers. Then simulate crank signals and faults on a bench. Controlled engine calibration precedes logging-only water trials. Bounded interventions follow only after ride interpretation and fault behaviour have been evaluated.

table.caption: Proposed validation gates
rows: Exact components, supplier answers and acceptance criteria.
Timing, communication timeout, reset and disturbed-supply behaviour.
Synchronisation, spark timing, fuel pressure and thermal measurements.
Synchronized rider demand, motion, speed, RPM and fault records.
Defined requests, limits, recovery and rider consequences under a test plan.

sections.title: Define states before programming transitions
sections.text: OFF, SELF CHECK, READY, CRANKING, RUNNING, DEGRADED and STOPPED / FAULT describe the proposed sequence. Each state needs permitted outputs, entry and exit conditions and event records. READY is not permission to energise ignition or injection. The simplified arrows below do not replace a complete transition specification.

sections.title: Specify fault responses physically
sections.text: A stop request, loss of crank synchronisation or implausible throttle input is different from losing optional navigation data. Define which outputs remain valid, the permitted demand, how the transition happens and how recovery is authorised. Do not call a fallback safe without evidence.

table.caption: Fault decisions to define and test — no thresholds approved
rows: Stop chain and ECU: stop thrust generation and inhibit unintended restart.
ECU: suppress invalid timing outputs and define restart checks.
ECU: reject stale requests and apply the tested baseline or limit policy.
ECU where supported: response matched to severity, persistence and load.
VCS: disable affected inferred strategies while preserving essential engine control.
Defined supervisor and power design: test output state, restart and isolation behaviour.

sections.title: Recovery is a separate decision
sections.text: Define whether a fault clears automatically, latches until power cycling or needs service. Returning CAN messages must not automatically restore an aggressive previous mode. Restart and recovery should be deliberate, observable and consistent with rider input.

sections.title: Keep a reproducible record
sections.text: Log test ID and time, engine/pump configuration, fuel and oil, controller and firmware revisions, calibration checksum, sensor calibration, rider/load, water conditions and objective. Align timestamps. Distinguish measured values from estimates and requested commands from actual actuator feedback.

sections.title: Publish evidence when it exists
sections.text: Define limits, response times and abort conditions before each test, using selected-component specifications and calibrator input. Preserve failed as well as successful runs. A brief successful run is not durability evidence, and a ride logger is not a substitute for timing measurements on the bench.
